image_description: Circular ring-shaped rash with raised scaly border and clear center on skin
input: Patient has a circular ring-shaped rash with a raised, scaly red border and a clearer center on their torso. Mild itching reported. No fever. Present for about 1 week.
expected_output: Possible ringworm (Tinea Corporis). Recommend consulting a doctor for antifungal treatment. Avoid sharing towels or clothing. Do not scratch the affected area.
context: Tinea Corporis (ringworm) is a fungal infection causing circular, ring-shaped rashes with raised scaly borders.
It is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact or contaminated surfaces.
Treatment typically involves topical antifungal creams prescribed by a doctor.
It is not caused by a worm despite the name.

image_description: Normal healthy skin on arm, no rash or lesions visible
input: Patient presents with normal-looking skin on their arm. No visible rash, redness, or lesions. Patient reports mild occasional dryness but no itching or pain.
expected_output: No visible skin condition detected. Skin appears healthy. If dryness persists, recommend a basic moisturizer. Consult a doctor if any new symptoms develop.
context: Healthy skin should have uniform tone without redness, lesions, or rashes.
Mild dryness can be managed with over-the-counter moisturizers.
Monitoring is recommended if new symptoms appear.

image_description: Large bullseye rash on shoulder/back area with concentric rings of redness
input: Patient has a large circular rash on their shoulder with a bullseye pattern — red center, lighter ring, then outer red ring. Appeared 4 days ago. Patient recently returned from a camping trip. Mild fatigue reported.
expected_output: Possible Lyme disease — bullseye rash (Erythema Migrans) is a hallmark sign. Seek urgent medical attention immediately. Do not wait for symptoms to worsen. Early antibiotic treatment is critical.
context: Erythema Migrans (bullseye rash) is the classic early sign of Lyme disease.
Lyme disease is transmitted through infected tick bites, common after outdoor/camping activities.
Early treatment with antibiotics (doxycycline) is highly effective.
Delayed treatment can lead to serious complications affecting joints, heart, and nervous system.
This is a medical emergency requiring immediate doctor consultation.

image_description: Clustered red raised bumps in groups on skin, resembling shingles or psoriasis
input: Patient has clusters of small red raised bumps grouped together on their back. Painful and itchy. Appeared suddenly 3 days ago. Patient is over 50 years old and reports feeling tired.
expected_output: Possible shingles (Herpes Zoster) or psoriasis. Given the clustered pattern and patient age, shingles is a concern. Seek medical attention promptly. Antiviral medication is most effective when started within 72 hours of rash onset.
context: Shingles is caused by reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (chickenpox virus).
It presents as painful clustered blisters/bumps typically on one side of the body.
Most common in people over 50 or those with weakened immunity.
Antiviral treatment must be started within 72 hours for maximum effectiveness.
Psoriasis presents as red scaly plaques and is a chronic autoimmune condition.

image_description: Dry, scaly, thickened skin patches on wrist/forearm area
input: Patient has dry, rough, scaly patches on their wrist and forearm. Skin appears thickened and cracked. Persistent itching, worse at night. Has had this for several months. No fever.
expected_output: Possible eczema (Atopic Dermatitis) or chronic contact dermatitis. Recommend consulting a dermatologist. Avoid known irritants like harsh soaps. Use fragrance-free moisturizers regularly. Do not scratch as it can worsen the condition.
context: Atopic Dermatitis (eczema) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition causing dry, itchy, scaly patches.
Common locations include wrists, inner elbows, and behind knees.
Triggers include soaps, detergents, stress, and environmental allergens.
Treatment includes topical corticosteroids (prescription), moisturizers, and avoiding triggers.
Chronic scratching can thicken the skin further (lichenification).

image_description: Two overlapping circular ring-shaped rashes with raised scaly borders on skin
input: Patient has two overlapping circular ring-shaped rashes on their leg. Both have raised, scaly, red borders. Has been spreading over the past 2 weeks. Patient has a pet cat at home.
expected_output: Possible ringworm (Tinea Corporis) — multiple lesions suggest spreading infection. Likely transmitted from pet. Recommend urgent dermatologist consultation for prescription antifungal treatment. The pet should also be examined by a veterinarian.
context: Ringworm is highly contagious and can spread from animals (especially cats and dogs) to humans.
Multiple spreading lesions indicate the infection is progressing and requires prescription treatment.
Topical antifungals may not be sufficient for multiple or spreading lesions — oral antifungals may be needed.
All household members and pets should be checked for infection.
Good hygiene practices are essential to prevent further spread.
